stops.name: Antioch, the cell, the small demon, and the hammer (the eastern glass)
stops.campa: Seen through Byzantine eyes the same cell holds a different enemy: not a great serpent but a small black demon that creeps to Marina, for so the East calls her, of-the-sea, in the dark to frighten her from her faith. She finds a copper hammer forgotten in the corner of the dungeon, seizes the demon by the horns, sets her foot on his neck, and beats him until he begs. Where the West paints a dragon and a hand-cross, the East paints a hammer and a devil small enough for one woman's sandal: the same cell, the same night, another set of eyes.
stops.quote: Depart from me, O lawless one.
stops.quote_source: Greek Synaxarion, Vita of the Great Martyr Marina (17 July)

stops.name: Antioch, the vat of water, and the dove (the eastern glass)
stops.campa: Where the western record has iron combs and a dragging rope, the eastern vita has Marina bound and lowered into a great vat of water to drown her before the crowd: the same threatened drowning her sister-timeline Margaret suffers by a sealed vessel. A white dove descends from the opened air, and with it a great light; her bonds fall away of themselves, and she rises from the vat healed of every wound, not a scar left on her, to the astonishment of the guards who had tied the knots that same morning.

stops.name: Antioch, the beheading (the eastern glass)
stops.campa: The eastern day ends where the western day ends, at the same hour, on the same ground: the governor, seeing his authority dissolve with every convert who has watched a girl walk unmarked out of fire, water, and a dragon's belly, orders her head struck off outside the city. The Greek calendar keeps her on the seventeenth of July as Great Martyr and Vanquisher of Demons, hammer in hand in her icons where the West gives her a cross: two glasses turned on one flame, the coronal light of one stop reappearing here as a nimbus over Marina's head.

stops.name: Antioch, the soldiers at the door
stops.campa: In the early fourth century, in a Christian household of Antioch, a girl of fifteen named Pelagia is at home when soldiers come pounding at the door, sent, though the brief record does not say by whom, only that persecution is loose in the city again, to take her, virgin and unmarried, for whatever use soldiers in such an hour intend. She hears them on the stair. Ambrose of Milan and John Chrysostom will later preach her as a model of chastity defended by any means necessary, including the last one; the household has only the length of the staircase to decide.

stops.name: Antioch, the leap from the housetop
stops.campa: Rather than be taken, Pelagia asks leave to change her dress, climbs to the top of the house, and without hesitating throws herself from the roof to the street below. She dies of the fall, fifteen years old, choosing the one door still hers to open. The record is almost too brief to be a story: a girl, a rooftop, a decision made faster than the soldiers can climb the stairs, and it is exactly that brevity the church keeps and reveres: no debate, no argument, only a body given entire rather than divided.
stops.quote: When a group of soldiers came to arrest her, this girl of fifteen threw herself from the top of the house, and died.
stops.quote_source: Henschel, dictionary 'Los Santos' (cited in the essay tradition); cf. Ambrose, De Virginibus III

stops.name: Antioch, the homilies of Ambrose and Chrysostom
stops.campa: Decades on, two of the greatest voices of the fourth-century church take up Pelagia's leap as doctrine. In Milan, Ambrose holds her before his consecrated virgins as proof that chastity may be defended by any means, even a death chosen outright. In Antioch itself, John Chrysostom, still a priest of his own city, preaches her memory to the same streets she fell through, praising the girl who out-argued her executioners by never letting them speak to her at all. Two bishops, two cities, one falling body: the church's first attempt to make doctrine of a leap it will not explain away.

stops.name: Antioch, the courtesan called Margaret
stops.campa: A woman older than the dragon-life and later than the leap moves through the same city under a third water: an actress and courtesan of Antioch, foremost and noblest of its women, dressed in nothing the Golden Legend can name without listing gold, silver, and precious stones. She goes by Margaret: for the pomp of my clothing, she will say of herself, though it is not the name of her baptism, which no one in the city yet knows. Vain and variable of courage, not chaste of body, she is, the chronicle insists, still herself entire, waiting for a reason to change.
stops.quote: For the pomp of my clothing men call me Margaret.
stops.quote_source: Golden Legend, Life of St. Pelagia; cf. essays/215_runaway_bride.md

stops.name: Antioch, the synod, and Nonnus of Heliopolis
stops.campa: A council of bishops gathers in Antioch, among them Nonnus, bishop of Heliopolis: Barbara's own city, whose stone tower stands two hundred kilometers south of this street, its arc touching Margaret's without either woman knowing it. Margaret passes the assembled fathers in procession, borne on a litter, scented, jeweled, laughing with her companions, careless of the churchmen's stares. Nonnus alone cannot look away; delighted and troubled at once by her hair and the shape of her body through the silk, he weeps before his brothers that he has not brought God so rich an offering in a single day's prayer as this woman brings her own vanity.
stops.quote: The adornments and array of one common woman hath surmounted in one day all the wisdom of all my life.
stops.quote_source: Golden Legend (Caxton, 1483), Life of St. Pelagienne

stops.name: Antioch, she seeks Nonnus, and throws herself into mercy
stops.campa: Struck by what she overhears of Nonnus's grief, Margaret comes herself to the church door and sends in asking for him. He will not receive her alone, keeping the other fathers present as witnesses against his own reported weakness, and she is made to wait outside the very walls that keep other women in. When admitted at last, she falls at his feet before the assembled clergy, weeping, and begs the baptism that will unmake the name Margaret and give her back the name her parents chose before either of her lives began: Pelagia, of the open sea.

stops.name: Antioch, the baptism under the birth name
stops.campa: Nonnus baptizes her himself, before the bishops of the synod, under the name Pelagia: not Margaret, the pomp-name, but the water-name, of-the-open-sea, the third of this life's names to carry that same tide. She gives every jewel, every garment of gold and silver, to the poor of Antioch through Nonnus's hand, keeping nothing back, the pearl divesting itself of every pearl it ever wore. The city that knew her as the richest of its women watches her walk out of the church in plain wool, and does not yet know whether to call it scandal or miracle.

stops.name: Antioch, the devil at the door, driven off
stops.campa: In the small room Nonnus has found her, the devil comes to Pelagia in the night in her old shape, reminding her of the silks and the litter and the men who paid to watch her walk. She answers him with the sign of the cross alone, no argument, no bargaining: the same gesture that once burst a dragon and once felled a demon under a sandaled foot, deployed now against a subtler enemy than either. He flees the room as the dragon fled the cross inside Margaret's body, and Pelagia is left alone with the wool dress and the decision still ahead of her.

stops.name: Antioch, the garment of Nonnus, and the flight to Jerusalem
stops.campa: Before dawn Pelagia takes one of Nonnus's own garments, a monk's habit, man's clothing, the cut hair implied though the Legend does not linger on it, and slips out of Antioch alone, leaving no household, no dowry, no farewell to the companions who knew her rich. She turns south and east toward Jerusalem, toward the Mount of Olives, three hundred kilometers of road walked as a man walks it, under a name now doubly hers: Pelagia to the church that baptized her, and soon Pelagius to the brothers who will never learn otherwise while she lives.
